audits.title: Fishery products

recommendations.text: Competent Authority The tasks allocated to all departments involved in supervision of fish and fishery products should be clearly identified. In view of the reorganisation taking place, any changes in responsibilities should be communicated to the Commission Services once they come into force.

Legislation All of the necessary legislation should be enacted and implemented in order to ensure that standards equivalent to EU requirements are achieved, in particular the legislation regarding the health conditions for the production and placing on the market of fishery products as well as the legislation concerning the quality of potable water.

Laboratories The official laboratory should be able to carry out the required microbiological and chemical analyses on fishery products, ice and water. Analysis of potable water should be carried out according to the relevant Community legislation. 19 The laboratory infrastructure should be adapted to the kind of analyses performed. In case of subcontracting, action should be taken to ensure that requirements set out in the contract are fulfilled.

Fish Farming Licenses and Approval of Establishments The procedure defined in Maltese legislation for the issuing of fish farming licenses should be applied. The procedure for approval, suspension and withdrawal of approval of establishments should be properly applied. In this respect, the list of approved establishments provided to the mission team should be updated, omitting both the fishery product establishment and the fish market. In view of possible future activities, it is recommended to allocate one unique approval number to the fish packing establishments only instead of to the farms as well.

Official Supervision Official supervision should be strengthened both at farm level and from the central level. In fish farms supervision on veterinary treatments as well as on drug store management should immediately be correctly carried out. In the establishments adequate supervision should be put in place to ensure correction of the deficiencies noted by the mission team. Therefore additional training in general hygiene issues as well as HACCP should be provided to all inspectors involved. In view of the potential risk of the types of products processed in the processing establishment and the lack of relevant analyses and of effective official supervision, approval of this establishment should be suspended. Written reporting procedures for the inspections carried out should be established. Analysis of water and ice should be carried out according to the provisions laid down by the relevant Community legislation.

Residue Monitoring Programme The residue monitoring programme should be carried out as described. Results should be correctly communicated. Targeted samplings should be performed and the sampling procedure should be applied according to the relevant Community legislation.
Export Health Certificate The competent authority should establish a procedure for issuing export health certificates according to the requirements laid down in the relevant Community legislation. 20
Fish Farms/Establishments All the deficiencies observed in the farms and the establishments should be rectified and for the latter, the drafted HACCP plans should be implemented.

Written guarantees The competent authority of Malta should forward to the European Commission written guarantees in respect of the rectification of all the points listed above within three months after having received the final report. More specifically for the drug store management, guarantees regarding corrective action taken should be forwarded immediately. The Competent Authority should also provide detailed information on the action that has been and will be taken and on the deadlines by which this action has been or will be completed. 8.2. To the Commission Services The Commission Services should not propose that Malta be put in list I of the Annex of the amended Commission Decision 97/296/EC. In view of the findings concerning the veterinary treatments and drug store management on the fish farms on the one hand, and the problems related to the residue monitoring programme on the other hand, the Commission Services should perform a thorough evaluation of this programme, its results as well as the written guarantees provided by the Maltese Competent Authority. 21 ADDENDUM TO THE MISSION REPORT DG SANCO/1048/2000 Answer of the competent authority to the recommendations of the report The Maltese competent authority has responded in full to the recommendations of the report. Their comments will be published with the final report on the Internet site of the Directorate-General Health and Consumer Protection. The deadline indicated by the competent authority for completion of the corrective actions is variable for the different issues: - Competent authority (8.1.1): a code of practices has been prepared - Legislation (8.1.2): legislation regarding the health conditions for the production and placing on the market of fishery products will be enacted and implemented not later than October 2000. Legislation on the quality of potable water will be issued during the year 2001 - Laboratories (8.1.3): action is being taken to ensure fulfilment with Community legislation - Fish farming licences and approval of establishments (8.1.4): the CA reviews the issuing procedure of fish farming licenses. A `new' list of approved establishments has been presented - Official supervision (8.1.5): measures have been taken to correct deficiencies and non-compliance - Residue monitoring programme (8.1.6): the programme is being reviewed - Export health certificate (8.1.7): the issuing procedure has been amended - Fish farms and establishments (8.1.8): action is being undertaken. The Maltese competent authority will inform the Commission services about the progress and exact time frame for the completion of these actions. 22

To take urgent action in order to improve staffing levels and overall performance of official supervision including enforcement of HACCP systems.

In their response to the draft report the Maltese Authorities stated that "It is important to clarify that a movement permit is not a movement record. In Malta a permit (valid for 7 days) allows movement between farms. Once the farmer moves the animal within the 7 day period both the seller and the buyer have to sign the report and forward it immediately to the Animal Health Unit. Controls are actually carried out by support staff once notification takes place and further controls are carried out through random controls. A final check is carried out at the slaughter once the farmer presents the slaughter document. If the slaughter document is not in place then premiums are not paid". 14 (3) To improve operational hygiene, maintenance and system of own checks, in particular testing of water quality, in all food establishments.

To ensure that controls on the supply of sheep milk for cheese production from raw milk, particularly in regard to tuberculosis testing and hygienic controls, are brought into line with Council Directive 92/46/EEC.

The Maltese authorities should submit an action plan including detailed actions and deadlines for their implementation to address the above recommendations within one month of receiving the final report. audits.title: Pesticides

recommendations.text: The competent authority should ensure that Council Directive 91/414/EEC is fully and accurately transposed.
The competent authority should ensure sufficient staffing for the evaluation and authorisation of plant protection products in the framework of Council Directive 91/414/EEC.

The competent authority should ensure that authorisations of plant protection products, as communicated to the applicant and as published in the Maltese Official Gazette, should be clear and unambiguous, and should specify the conditions relating to the placing on the market and use of the product in accordance with Article 4.2 of Council Directive 91/414/EEC. The competent authority should ensure that the packaging and labelling of plant protection products satisfies the requirements specified in Articles 15 and 16 of Council Directive 91/414/EEC, and requirements for packaging and labelling should be included in the authorisation certificate.
The competent authority should ensure that plant protection products are classified and labelled fully in accordance with Directive 1999/45/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council.

The competent authority should review authorisations of plant protection products following the inclusion and non-inclusion of active substances in Annex I of Council Directive 91/414/EEC within the specified timelines.

The competent authority should systematically follow-up infringements recorded during the controls of the marketing of plant protection products. They should also establish controls of the uses of plant protection products, including follow-up, in accordance with Article 17 of Council Directive 91/414/EEC.
The competent authority should submit an annual report to the Commission in the framework of Article 17 of Council Directive 91/414/EEC.
The competent authorities should ensure that sampling is carried out fully in accordance with Commission Directive 2002/63/EC, and inspectors should be trained in sampling requirements.

In cases of MRL infringements, the competent authorities should carry out systematic consumer risk assessments taking also into account the draft "Proposal on how to notify 20 pesticide residues in foodstuffs in the Rapid Alert System for Foodstuffs" (SANCO/3346/2001).

The competent authorities should ensure that any information relating to a risk to human health from pesticide residues is notified without delay to the national contact point for the Rapid Alert System, in accordance with Article 50 of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002 of the European Parliament and of the Council. An action plan in response to the recommendations should be forwarded to the Commission within 2 months of dispatch of the final report. This action plan should clearly set out the manner and deadline by which the competent authorities will address each recommendation. 9. recommendations.text: To ensure that the veterinary checks in the BIP are implemented under the responsibility of the official veterinarian as required by Article 4(1) of Directive 97/78/EC and that, after completion of the required veterinary checks, the certificate for the consignments concerned certifying the results of the checks is only issued and signed by the official veterinarian, as required by Article 5(1) of Directive 97/78/EC.

citations.text: The competent authority has written job descriptions for the official veterinarians and the veterinary support staff. These include the general responsibilities of the personnel and they do not detail specific tasks and related responsibilities (finding 17) contrary to the requirement of Chapter II(4) of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. In this context, it was noted that auxiliary staff carry out controls and sign certificates when such activities have not been included in their responsibilities. This shortcoming was reported in the 2010 report and a recommendation (No 3) was consequently issued, which has not been addressed.

The competent authority complies with the requirements of communication, training and instructions (with the exception of instructions for control of transhipments and for sampling for microbiological testing) and resources to support the effective implementation of the controls. However, the system does not ensure veterinary checks and certification are only performed by authorised staff which may lead to imports of consignments that do not fulfil the legal requirements related to animal and/or public health.

Previous FVO audits identified that veterinary checks and issuing of certificates were not always done by authorised staff (see finding 4). After the 2010 FVO audit the competent authority hired an additional official veterinarian but the shortcoming had not been addressed at the time of the 2011 audit (see heading 5.2.1 of the 2011 report). The situation remains unchanged, auxiliary staff carrying out controls when official 6 veterinarians are not present in the BIPs and signing subsequent certificates (CVEDs) in TRACES.

The audit team noted that in the port BIP official controls and the signing/issuing of CVEDs was done by the official veterinarians. In the airport BIP the official veterinarian is present once per week and support staff performs more than 95% of the official import controls, including the signing/issuing of CVEDs. Official veterinarians are not involved in the performance of official controls to ensure that they are correctly implemented. This means that: Official controls are not performed under the responsibility of the official veterinarian contrary to the requirements of article 4(1) of Directive 97/78/EC; The signing of CVEDs, is done by support staff instead of the official veterinarians which is not in line with Article 5 of Directive 97/78/EC. Although this non- compliance was identified in the 2011 FVO report, the competent authority has not addressed it in order to have only official veterinarians signing the CVEDs.

Import controls are implemented but the systemic problems identified in previous FVO audits remain unaddressed: pre-notification of consignments does not include all the information required, the competent authority does not ensure that no entry or handling of veterinary consignments occurs in the free zone of the port without their agreement, controls are not implemented by authorised staff (including the issuing of certificates), the monitoring plan has a limited scope. As regards transhipments, the competent authority has access to information (Customs information, manifests) but does not use it to identify the goods and the required controls on consignments transhipping in Malta are not implemented. The above undermine the capability of the system to prevent the introduction to the Union market of consignments that do not meet the requirements of the import legislation.

In one slaughterhouse (and in the CCA office) the approval file did not include any document. The same situation was found at the time of the 2007, 2009 and 2013 DG Health and Food Safety audits. The FBO later provided a letter issued by the CA on 20 December 2019, stating that the operator was "hereby being approved to run an abattoir"; a copy of such document was not included in the approval file kept in the CCA office, and both the FBO and the CA were unable to demonstrate that this letter was issued following an application. The slaughterhouse had undergone extensive refurbishments and changes in equipment (including the building of a new facility for emergency slaughter) since the last DG Health and Food Safety audit in 2013, which had identified relevant structural and hygienic non-conformities. However, the absence of a blueprint on file makes impossible to identify which parts have been refurbished and which areas and equipment are covered by the approval. Moreover, being a multispecies slaughterhouse, no maximum capacity or slaughter line speed have been set for the different animal species slaughtered in order to ensure appropriate hygienic slaughter practices. b. The cutting premises that were built later within the vicinity of the slaughterhouse described above were first conditionally approved and definitely approved in 2016: documentation related to the inspections that were carried out during the approval process was available on file. However, the blue print was not on file, making the evaluation of structures, equipment, and flow of carcases-final products-personnel difficult to evaluate. The approval did not indicate maximum capacities for cutting, nor did it set any restriction for middlemen who were still allowed to enter the premises with their own equipment and operate on the carcases. c. The cutting premises that were built later in the vicinity of the second slaughterhouse visited, were first conditionally approved and definitely approved in 2017: however, also in this case, no blueprint of the premises and equipment, nor maximum capacity allowed for cutting were documented. The attached slaughterhouse had been granted a flexibility measure in May 2017 related to the frequency of carcases testing for aerobic bacteria, Salmonella and Enterobacteriaceae counts. The FBO had been allowed to carry out such tests fortnightly on cattle and swine carcases, but not on small ruminants carcases. However, Article 5(3) of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 only allows FBOs to benefit from such flexibility when they are able to demonstrate implementation of effective HACCP-based procedures supported by good results from several sampling sessions. Neither the two OVs, who were in charge of official tasks at the premises since 2017, nor the senior OV responsible for their supervision had enforced these preconditions. In fact, the FBO had never tested carcases against the microbiological criteria set in the Regulation: such non-compliance was only detected on 22 November 2019 during an audit carried out by the CCA (the first 8 within a three years period). To date, the requirement is not yet enforced; the FBO could only demonstrate having received a quotation from an accredited laboratory for a suitable testing scheme. d. The last establishment visited was definitively approved as a cold store, and has been conditionally approved since December 2019 for re-packing activities and for producing meat cuts, meat preparations and minced meat. recommendations.text: To ensure availability of, or have access to, a sufficient number of qualified and experienced staff to carry out efficient and effective official controls and other official activities, as required by Article 5(1)(e) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: At the time of the audit there were 11 unfilled posts for veterinary officers at the VRD, and to manage the workload, several officers had taken on additional duties, working only half time for their original job description without having been provided with specific training for their new tasks. The ABP Section has undergone frequent staff changes in recent years and two of the three officers in the ABP Section (one is on long term leave) are dividing their working time between controls on feedingstuffs and ABP.

The VRD has staff shortages in several of its Units, including the FSCU and its ABP Section. This has resulted in a higher workload for the ABP Section and failure to meet the annual targets for control frequencies. The situation is impaired by frequent staff turnover in the ABP Section, lack of specific procedures for some ABP control areas and lack of training on ABP organised in the last five years. The numerous weaknesses noted during the audit related to the approval of ABP plants (see section 5.2.) and the shortcomings noted at practically all of the sites visited by the audit team (see section 5.3.3.) indicate that the staff of the ABP Section have insufficient knowledge of the specific requirements for ABP and DP laid down in the EU legislation and thus compromises their ability to carry out effective official controls, in particular regarding requirements for incinerators and biogas plants.

The audit team noted significant shortcomings regarding the registration, approval and listing of ABP plants, establishments and operators. The interviewed staff of the ABP Section stated that these problems were due to frequent staff turnover, prioritisation of other tasks, a lack of resources and the absence of handover procedures of the respective files for approval, registration and listing. With regard to the approval and registration of ABP plants and operators: a) Whilst the biogas plant visited by the audit team has had an operation permit from the Malta Environment and Planning Authority (MEPA) since 2015, it has not been subject to an on-site visit before commencement of its activities as required by Article 44(1) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 and has been operating without an approval contrary to the requirement of Article 24(g) of the same Regulation. It also does not have a pasteurisation/hygienisation unit as required in point 1, Section 1, 10 Chapter 1 of Annex V to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011 and the plant operator had not provided the competent authority with the guarantees that would allow a derogation to be made (point 2 of the above Section 1) from this requirement. b) According to the VRD statement there are four temporary storage points collecting liquid slurry. A part of the slurry is delivered from these points to the biogas plant, the rest is going into the sewage. The VRD has neither registered, nor approved, these facilities as ABP storage plants. c) One of the ABP incinerators visited had a valid environmental operation permit from the MEPA and was equipped with two lines for thermal treatment of ABP (one line for Category 3 material and one for mixture of the Category 1 and 2 material). The operator stated that an initial plan was to trade the derived fats and meat and bone meal produced on these lines, but so far the derived fats and meat and bone meal derived after the thermal treatment were all incinerated without being permanently marked. This is not in line with point 3(d) of Chapter V of Annex VIII to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011 which allows for derogating from marking the products only if these are moved from the processing plant for direct incineration by a closed conveyer system, which may not be by-passed, and that such a system has been authorised by the competent authority. The above examples are not in line with Article 24 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009, which requires that the competent authority approves all ABP plants and operators that are in operation.

The ABP Section has conducted very few official controls in ABP plants and establishments in recent years and the planned frequency of controls has not been met. The ABP Section staff stated that this was due to staff shortages and other work priorities. The audit team noted that: a) The biogas plant has never been inspected and the main and only large-scale incinerator plant was last inspected in 2016. 12 b) There was no evidence that ABP transporters have ever been included in the annual work plans. c) An approved storage plant handling raw hides, was last inspected in December 2019, the previous inspection had taken place nine years earlier. d) The environmental health officers responsible for the controls of the butcher's shop visited stated that they do not cover ABP in their controls. citations.text: The few written records of official controls available for the establishments and plants visited at the end of 2019 or beginning of 2020 were very short and overall superficial - a number of non-compliances identified by the audit team had not been detected during the competent authority's controls in 2019 and 2020. 5.3.3.1 Official controls in the ABP plants

The official controls on ABP plants had not noted any serious shortcomings in relation to general hygiene conditions, operation and maintenance. However, the audit team still noted some shortcomings in the high-capacity incineration plant visited: a) The solid components of wastewater (Category 1 material) were pumped out to an approved site instead of disposing it using the methods allowed for this material under Article 12 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. If this shortcoming existed at the time of the previous inspection in 2016, it was not recorded in the report of said inspection. b) The meat and bone meal resulting from the thermal treatment preceding incineration was stored in large open vats with birds feeding from them. Furthermore there were many plastic containers in the yard without any identification. The operator stated that these contained rendered fats stored for incineration. The above is contrary to the requirement of points 3 and 5, Section 1, Chapter I of Annex III to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011 which require that animals must not have access to ABP that are awaiting for incineration and that these ABP must be covered, and correctly identified, respectively. If these shortcomings existed at the time of the previous inspection in 2016, they were not recorded in the report of said inspection.

Regarding controls on requirements on general hygiene, the audit team noted some shortcomings that had not been picked up during previous official controls: a) In the poultry slaughterhouse, blood was collected in vats to be disposed of in the high-capacity incinerator plant. However, blood ended up also in the drain of the slaughter hall and some of it was leaking out from the floor to the slaughterhouse surroundings. This is contrary to requirements laid in point 6 of Section 2 of Chapter I of Annex IV to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011, which prohibits disposal of blood through the waste stream. This had not been recorded as a shortcoming in the two annual control reports seen, the latest of November 2019 and was restricted to identification, traceability and transport of ABP. b) In the same slaughterhouse, the mechanical removal of SRM was not always complete. This shortcoming had been recorded in a 2018 inspection report which recommended the operator to take care of this shortcoming. However, no deadline was set by which this should have been corrected and there was no evidence of follow-up by the competent authority to verify that this had happened.

In the dairy establishment visited the permanent procedures based on the HACCP principles regarding ABP disposal included disposal of separator sludge and white wash water into the drains, instead of applying the methods provided for in Article 14 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. This had not been noted as a shortcoming in the report of an inspection carried out in 2019.

The official controls on ABP covered identification of ABP. The ABP storage plants and food business operators had arrangements in place to collect and identify ABP. Nonetheless, the audit team noted the following shortcomings in relation to identification of ABP which had not been identified in the records of official controls: a) Some of the containers designated and vehicles registered for transport of ABP to the high-capacity incinerator plant were not correctly identified and labelled; and b) In one of the cutting plants visited, ABP was collected in containers that were not correctly identified and labelled. 14 All the above are not in line with point 2 of Chapter II of Annex VIII to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011, requiring proper identification of handled ABP.

The audit team noted that the official controls in some of the establishments visited have not included the checks on records or, when they covered record keeping, did not detect a number of non-compliances related to the traceability requirements laid down in Article 22 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 and the relevant requirements of Chapter III of Annex VIII to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011. For example, in the dairy establishment visited, no commercial documents were available for the former foodstuffs and other ABP sent to landfill, which is contrary to the requirement of Article 21(2) and Article 22(1) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. There was no evidence that the official controls had identified this shortcoming.

recommendations.text: To ensure that the required number of isolates are obtained, and that sample size takes into consideration the estimated prevalence of the relevant bacteria, in line with Article 3 of and points 3 and 4.1 of part A of the Annex to Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2020/1729. ii, 5, 11iii and iv, 13iii, 14iv and 15iv.

citations.text: There were issues with the sampling plans, for the first 2 years of AMR monitoring under the EU Decision: i. The VRD only issued and distributed its standard operating procedure (SOP) for sampling 22 months after the monitoring was due to start (October 2022). ii. The SOP refers to a fixed number of 150 caecal samples based on the derogation applicable when there is low or unknown prevalence of certain bacterial species combined with low annual production. However, when prevalence is above 30%, another derogation requiring a minimum number of isolates is applicable. The SOP does not reflect this possibility and does not state that sampling needs to be done at 3 all BCPs (see point 15iv). This is not fully in line with points 3(1)(b), 3(3) and point 4(1) of part A of the Annex to the EU Decision. iii. The HIS' annual memo was issued late in 2021 (only in September) but the situation improved in 2022 (memo issued in February). For these 2 years the sampling design was not proportionately distributed between the population of the two geographical regions (see point 14ii) due to resource issues.

The responsible competent authorities are clearly designated and have the necessary powers to implement the monitoring of AMR. However, issues of capacity (mostly Covid-19 related) and coordination affected the development and implementation of annual planning in 2021 and 2022.

In 2021 and to some extent in 2022, issues with the development and implementation of the AMR monitoring plan (such as lack of resources and sampling procedures) affected the ability to achieve the minimum number of required samples and representativeness of retail meat samples. This resulted in a lower availability of isolates for some of the relevant combinations of bacteria and animal species. Nonetheless, most issues are not likely to persist in the coming years if the changes planned for 2023 are implemented.

recommendations.text: To ensure that the analytical methods for isolation and detection are in line with Article 3 and points 4 and 5 of Part A of Annex to Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2020/1729 and Article 37(5)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: The methods used by the PHL for fresh meat samples are not aligned with the EURL protocols. In particular, the deviations below are contrary to the requirements of points 4, 5 and 7 of Part A of the Annex to the EU Decision and affect the reliability of results: i. The selective isolation of CP-producing E. coli was not carried out in 2021 and 2022. Instead, the absence of meropenem resistance in isolates cultured on the Mac Conkey-CTX plates was used to establish the presence of presumptive CP-producing E. coli, which is not in line with the EURL recommended methods. As such there was no specific monitoring of CP-producing E. coli in place. ii. In relation to the method for isolation of ESBL-, AmpC- and CP-producing E. coli, the TBX plate was used as the identification step and source of isolates for storage and AST. However, this plate should only be used for selection and storage of isolates should be done from a non-selective plate.

The methods used by the NVL largely follow the relevant international standards. However, the audit team noted a few deviations which are not fully in line with points 4, 5 and 7 of part A of the Annex to the EU Decision and in some cases may affect the reliability of results, as follows: i. Carbapenem plates were not available for selective isolation of CP-producing E. coli, instead only OXA-48 plates were used in 2021 and 2022. This deviation from the recommended method decreases the sensitivity of the method. To correct this issue the Carbapenem plate has recently been introduced for specific monitoring for 2023. ii. The method used - Hippurate only - was insufficient to distinguish Campylobacter coli from Campylobacter lari. In the 2021 Campylobacter AST proficiency test, identification of Campylobacter jejuni was missed and the investigation was not documented (the NVL stated that this was due to the cause being known). Validation or proficiency tests have not been run for Campylobacter isolation due to the lack of a commercially available proficiency test in a suitable matrix.

Currently Malta's NRL for AMR is not accredited and does not perform all the required tasks of an NRL. This, coupled with deviations from the EURL recommended methods, storage of isolates and the lack of validation weakens the ability of Malta's official laboratories to correctly carry out testing and therefore diminishes the overall reliability of the data reported.

In both establishments, the operators carried out cross-contamination tests twice per year. In one compound feed producer manufacturing medicated feed, the operator carried out cross-contamination test on active substances twice per year. In one establishment, the feed inspectors met satisfactorily assessed the results of the cross-contamination tests but experienced difficulties in assessing the appropriateness of the sampling method adopted by the operator. recommendations.text: To ensure that official controls consistently check feed business operators' compliance with legislative requirements concerning the appropriateness of retained samples.
recommendations.legal_basis: part 4 of the section "Quality control" of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 183/2005.

citations.text: Routine inspections include a verification of operators' traceability systems, including the operators' obligation to take samples of ingredients and from each batch of products manufactured and placed on the market, or of each specific portion of production (in the case of continuous production) in sufficient quantities, using a procedure pre-established by the manufacturer (hereinafter `retained samples'). This is required in part 4 of the section" Quality control" of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 183/2005. The audit team scrutinised the operators' documentation on collection, packaging, labelling and storage of retained samples, interviewed the feed inspectors who usually control those establishments and made the following observations: · in two establishments, retained samples were not collected (and stored) from feed additives (amino acids); · in two establishments, retained samples were not adequately sealed; · in two establishments, FeBOs collected samples from incoming feed materials. These samples were used in their own laboratories to analyse different quality parameters and 5 the rest was kept as retained samples. Thus, the material was subject to diverse manipulations prior to being kept as retained samples; · in two feed material producers, the FeBOs consistently did not collect retained samples from each batch of produced feed material. These observations are not in line with the legal requirements established in part 4 of the section "Quality control" of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 183/2005 and were not identified in any of the inspection reports seen.

citations.text: The interpretation of the analytical results of official feed samples is the responsibility of FSAN officials based on the laboratory reports provided by testing laboratories. The audit team noted that the inspectors experienced significant difficulties in interpreting the laboratory test reports, in particular in taking into account the mandatory parameters (e.g., recalculation to feed with 12% moisture content, correction for recovery), required by point 6 of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 152/2009, to determine compliance. 5.2.2.2 Implementation of official sampling

citations.text: In particular, the Food Safety Act is essential in the scope of the audit. citations.text: At the time of the audit, none of the laboratories for pharmacologically active sub- stances and for contaminants (non-retail samples) were appropriately designated as official laboratories by the VRD, contrary to EU requirements (50). Furthermore, some of the analytical methods used are not included in the laboratories' scope of accreditation as required by EU legislation (51). (52)

The NVL receives all samples taken by the VRD for testing for residues of pharma- cologically active substances and contaminants (with the exception of samples taken in the retail sector). It performs mixing and homogenisation of certain samples, stores samples and transfers them to the sub-contracted foreign laboratories.

The capability and performance of the laboratory network used for both pesticides and contaminants is fit for purpose. This is not the case for the sub-contracted la- boratories testing for residues of pharmacologically active substances. None were appropriately designated and some of the methods used were not included in their respective scopes of accreditation. Furthermore, some did not comply with the legal provisions for interpreting non-compliant results. There was an absence of data on the stability of analytes in matrix and substantial delays in the dispatch of stored samples from the NVL to the sub-contracted laboratories. Collectively these ele- ments substantially weaken the reliability of the results generated.
